analysis.one_liner: Requires all derivatives and swaps to trade on regulated exchanges instead of privately.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in the final weeks of a Congress in which the financial crisis had just peaked, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, drew zero cosponsors, and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Commodity Exchange Act to strike the legal exemptions that let most derivatives and swap deals trade privately, outside the reach of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Every such contract would instead have to run through a regulated exchange or regulated trading facility, and so-called exempt boards of trade would be abolished. It was introduced on November 20, 2008, weeks after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, by Senator Tom Harkin, and died without a hearing in the Senate Agriculture Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit indirectly: taxpayers, savers, pension holders, and anyone whose job or mortgage depends on a stable financial system, because opaque private derivatives markets were a central cause of the 2008 crisis. Farmers, airlines, and energy users who depend on commodity prices would also benefit from trading that is visible and harder to manipulate, as would regulators who currently cannot see who owes what to whom.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the legal exemptions that allowed most derivative and swap transactions to trade outside CFTC regulation, ending the 'legalized off-exchange' status they had under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000.

It restricts futures trading to regulated contract markets or derivatives transaction execution facilities, so pricing and trading would be visible to regulators and to the public instead of negotiated privately.

It abolishes exempt boards of trade and strikes the exemptions in Commodity Exchange Act sections 2(d), 2(e), 2(g), 2(h), 2(i) and 4(c) — the provisions that had kept swaps and other derivatives from oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and dealers who profit from over-the-counter swaps trading would pay: they would lose the private, unregulated dealing business and face exchange rules, margin requirements, and fees. Companies that hedge with customized private contracts — airlines, food processors, manufacturers — would face higher costs and less flexibility.

drawbacks.text: Requiring every derivatives contract to trade on a regulated exchange is a one-size-fits-all mandate: businesses with genuinely customized hedging needs — airlines locking in fuel prices, food companies locking in crop costs — would lose the ability to negotiate tailored private contracts and would face exchange fees, margin requirements, and standardized terms instead.
A ban on off-exchange derivatives could push some trading offshore to foreign venues with no US oversight, unless coordinated internationally — a problem the bill text does not address.

The bill was drafted hastily in the weeks after Lehman Brothers collapsed and drew no cosponsors from either party, including from Harkin's fellow Democrats, so it was never tested in a hearing or amended in response to industry or expert criticism.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill was straightforward after a crisis caused in part by unregulated derivatives: forcing every swap onto a regulated exchange would make pricing visible, create a record of who owed what to whom, and give regulators real-time data, at the cost of some flexibility for legitimate hedgers. The case against was that a one-size-fits-all mandate could raise hedging costs for companies managing real business risks and risk pushing some trading to overseas venues with no US oversight at all — a real trade-off an honest supporter would have to acknowledge. On balance, the consumer-protection and stability gains were the bill's stated purpose, and the flexibility costs were the main honest objection. The bill itself was never weighed in a hearing or vote, so the record contains only the argument for it, not a tested answer to the objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and stayed there — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — until that Congress ended three months later.

narrative.text: Introduced November 20, 2008 — seven weeks before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 — the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which took no further action on it.
The bill never gained a single cosponsor, from either party, during its lifetime.

The proposal targeted the exemptions created by the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000, which had allowed most derivatives and swaps to trade outside regulation; two years later, Congress imposed exchange-trading and clearing requirements for many swaps in the Dodd-Frank Act — a different bill, with a different fate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks and swaps dealers whose unregulated, privately negotiated derivatives business was untouched: the bill died with zero cosponsors and no hearing, so the status quo they operated under continued until replaced by different legislation two years later.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 20, 2008, delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor, and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: 110th Senate
against.what_they_did: No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor in the bill's seven weeks of life, and the Congress ended without floor action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor from either party joined, so the partisan shape of the idea was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Big banks and OTC swaps dealers
industries.note: Dealers earned large fees trading privately negotiated swaps outside exchanges, where pricing was opaque and no exchange margin or clearing rules applied. The bill forces every derivative onto a regulated exchange, eliminating that fee stream and imposing oversight. Their interest ran against the public's: the opacity they profited from was the very thing the bill was written to fix after the 2008 crisis.
Trading that had been done privately would have to move onto regulated exchanges or derivatives transaction execution facilities, creating new business for them.

industries.industry: Exempt boards of trade and unregulated electronic trading facilities
industries.note: The bill repeals section 5d of the Commodity Exchange Act and strikes the electronic-trading-facility exemptions, ending these venues' legal status for off-exchange derivatives trading.

They would gain transparency and lower counterparty risk on the trades they keep, but lose the ability to privately negotiate customized derivative contracts and would face exchange margin and fee requirements.
